questions.q: Why does SQL Server need a separate lock category for a table's schema, apart from locks on its data?
options: Because a column disappearing mid-query is a different, more disruptive problem than a row being edited mid-query
Because schema locks are actually identical to row locks
Because SQL Server only has one lock type total, and this is it
Because DDL statements never run inside transactions
questions.explain: Structural changes mid-query (like a dropped column) are a fundamentally different hazard than data changes, so they get their own lock category.

questions.q: When is a schema stability (Sch-S) lock taken?
options: Automatically during normal query compilation and execution, essentially every time a statement runs against a table
Only when a DBA explicitly requests it
Only during ALTER TABLE statements
Only once per server restart
questions.explain: Sch-S is taken routinely during ordinary query execution to guarantee the table's structure doesn't change while the query runs.

questions.q: What is a schema modification (Sch-M) lock compatible with?
options: Nothing — it is incompatible with everything, including Sch-S
Other Sch-M locks only
Sch-S locks, but not data locks
All shared and intent locks
questions.explain: Sch-M is deliberately incompatible with everything, including Sch-S, so a structural change can't happen while any query is mid-execution against that table.

questions.q: Why can an ordinary SELECT end up blocking an ALTER TABLE statement running against the same table?
options: The SELECT holds a Sch-S lock, and Sch-M (needed by ALTER TABLE) conflicts with Sch-S, so ALTER TABLE waits for the SELECT to finish
SELECT statements always take a Sch-M lock
ALTER TABLE never actually needs any lock
SELECT and ALTER TABLE can never run against the same table at all
questions.explain: Because Sch-M conflicts with Sch-S in both directions, a long-running SELECT can delay a structural change just as easily as the reverse.

questions.q: What is the practical, real-world symptom of Sch-M and Sch-S being mutually exclusive?
options: An ALTER TABLE against a busy table can appear to hang while waiting for in-flight queries to finish, and vice versa
ALTER TABLE statements always fail instantly with an error
SELECT statements silently return stale data instead of waiting
Nothing — schema locks have no observable effect on query behavior
questions.explain: This mutual exclusivity is exactly why DDL changes are often scheduled during low-traffic windows.
